```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", fig.retina = 2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# Paths are relative to the vignette/ folder
dat     <- read.csv("../data/numeric_GPA3_0_first.csv")
res     <- read.csv("../output/results.csv")
bal     <- read.csv("../output/balance.csv")
dat$age[dat$age == 0] <- NA   # age = 0 codes a missing value

alpha <- 0.10

# Readable labels for treatments and subgroups (as in Tables 3 to 7)
trt_labels <- c(
  "GPA 3.0 or below"                                    = "GPA ≤ 3.0",
  "PTSD score 33 or higher"                             = "PTSD score ≥ 33",
  "COVID isolation above 7"                             = "COVID-19 isolation > 7",
  "Three or more intense educational helpers"           = "Educational helpers ≥ 3",
  "Maximum emotional help 9 or higher"                  = "Max. emotional help ≥ 9",
  "Academic perseverance above median"                  = "Academic perseverance > median",
  "Not a cisgender woman"                               = "Not a cisgender woman",
  "Trauma score above median (higher = fewer events?)"  = "Trauma score > median",
  "Trauma score above median (fewer traumatic events)"  = "Trauma score > median"
)
grp_levels <- c("Full sample", "High PTSD (>=33)", "Low PTSD (<33)",
                "Cisgender women", "Cisgender men",
                "White", "Asian/Asian-American", "Other racial identity",
                "Ages 18-20", "Ages 21-24", "Ages 25+")
grp_labels <- c("Full sample", "High PTSD symptom severity", "Low PTSD symptom severity",
                "Cisgender women", "Cisgender men",
                "White students", "Asian/Asian-American students", "Students of other racial identities",
                "Ages 18–20", "Ages 21–24", "Ages 25+")

res <- res %>%
  mutate(Treatment = unname(trt_labels[treatment]),
         Group     = factor(grp_labels[match(group, grp_levels)], levels = grp_labels))

fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 1e-4, "< 0.0001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 4))
```

## Overview

This vignette documents the analysis behind the paper and reproduces every number
reported in its tables and supplementary materials. It is organised in the same
order as the analysis itself.

1. The analytic sample and the subgroups.
2. The treatment contrasts and how each is coded.
3. The causal estimand and identifying assumptions.
4. Propensity score estimation with XGBoost and inverse probability weighting.
5. Weighting diagnostics (Supplementary Table S2, Fig S1, S1 Data).
6. Treatment effect estimates (Tables 3 to 7).
7. The Benjamini and Hochberg adjustment.

The model-fitting step (step 4) requires the `xgboost` R package and is run by
`R/causal_ipw.R`, which writes the files in `output/`. This vignette reads those
saved outputs, so it renders without refitting the models, and it recomputes from
the raw data everything that does not depend on the fitted propensity scores.

To reproduce the full analysis from scratch:

```{bash, eval = FALSE}
# from the student-mh-causal/ folder
Rscript R/causal_ipw.R          # fits all 46 models, writes output/
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("vignette/vignette.Rmd")'
```

## 1. Data and analytic sample

The data come from an online survey of students at a large public university in the
Mid-Atlantic United States, administered between April 9 and June 3, 2020. The analytic
sample contains **`r nrow(dat)` students**, each with complete information on all study
variables except age, which is missing for `r sum(is.na(dat$age))` students.

The outcome, `mh_scale`, is the mean of the 21 items of the Depression Anxiety Stress
Scales (DASS-21). It ranges from 0 to 3, and higher values indicate greater psychological
distress.

```{r outcome}
ggplot(dat, aes(mh_scale)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.125, boundary = 0, fill = "#2C7FB8", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Mental Health Scale (DASS-21 item mean, higher = more distress)",
       y = "Number of students",
       title = sprintf("Outcome distribution (mean %.2f, SD %.2f)",
                       mean(dat$mh_scale), sd(dat$mh_scale))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### Subgroups

Analyses were run in the full sample and separately within subgroups defined by PTSD
symptom severity, gender identity, race, and age. Students identifying as gender
minorities (n = `r sum(dat$gender == 2)`) were too few for a separate gender stratum,
and age-stratified analyses use the `r sum(!is.na(dat$age))` students with recorded age.

```{r subgroups}
sub_n <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Stratification, ~Subgroup, ~n,
  "None",        "Full sample",                         nrow(dat),
  "PTSD",        "High symptom severity (PCL-5 ≥ 33)", sum(dat$ptsd_score >= 33),
  "PTSD",        "Low symptom severity (PCL-5 < 33)",   sum(dat$ptsd_score < 33),
  "Gender",      "Cisgender women",                     sum(dat$gender == 0),
  "Gender",      "Cisgender men",                       sum(dat$gender == 1),
  "Race",        "White",                               sum(dat$race == 0),
  "Race",        "Asian/Asian-American",                sum(dat$race == 2),
  "Race",        "Other racial identities",             sum(dat$race == 1),
  "Age",         "18–20",                          sum(dat$age <= 20, na.rm = TRUE),
  "Age",         "21–24",                          sum(dat$age %in% 21:24),
  "Age",         "25 and older",                        sum(dat$age >= 25, na.rm = TRUE)
)
kable(sub_n, caption = "Subgroup sample sizes") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed")) %>%
  collapse_rows(columns = 1, valign = "top")
```

## 2. Treatment definitions

Every exposure is dichotomized so that the average treatment effect (ATE) compares two
well-defined groups of students. The table gives the exact definition of the group coded 1,
the reason for the cutoff, and the number of treated students in the full sample,
computed directly from the data.

```{r treatments}
trt_tab <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Treatment, ~`Coded 1 if`, ~Justification, ~`Treated (full sample)`,
  "GPA ≤ 3.0", "Self-reported cumulative GPA at or below 3.0",
    "B average; standard benchmark for good academic standing", sum(dat$gpa_thresh3_0 == 1),
  "PTSD score ≥ 33", "PCL-5 total of 33 or higher (range 0–80)",
    "Recommended threshold for probable PTSD (Bovin et al., 2016); not a diagnosis", sum(dat$ptsd_score >= 33),
  "COVID-19 isolation > 7", "Isolation item above 7 (0 = strongly disagree, 10 = strongly agree)",
    "Clear agreement on a scale with neutral point 5; just above the sample median of 7", sum(dat$covid_iso > 7),
  "Educational helpers ≥ 3", "Three or more network members giving intense educational help",
    "Above the median of 2 intense educational helpers", sum(dat$edu.i_count >= 3),
  "Max. emotional help ≥ 9", "Highest emotional-help rating of any network member is 9 or 10",
    "At least one source of near-maximal emotional support", sum(dat$max.emohelp >= 9),
  "Academic perseverance > median", sprintf("Academic perseverance above %.1f (1–6 scale)", median(dat$acpers)),
    "Full-sample median split", sum(dat$acpers > median(dat$acpers)),
  "Not a cisgender woman", "Gender identity other than cisgender woman",
    "Used only within the PTSD strata", sum(dat$gender != 0),
  "Trauma score > median", sprintf("Trauma item sum above %d", as.integer(median(dat$trauma_sum))),
    "Full-sample median split. Higher scores mean FEWER reported traumatic experiences", sum(dat$trauma_sum > median(dat$trauma_sum))
)
kable(trt_tab, caption = "Treatment contrasts (group coded 0 is everyone else in the analytic sample)") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), font_size = 13)
```

The trauma score is scored in the reverse of what its name suggests. Its correlation
with the PCL-5 score is `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(dat$trauma_sum, dat$ptsd_score))` and with
the outcome `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(dat$trauma_sum, dat$mh_scale))`, so the trauma
indicator identifies students reporting comparatively *less* trauma exposure.

Which treatments are examined in which stratum:

```{r plan}
res %>%
  distinct(Group, Treatment) %>%
  mutate(x = "✓") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Treatment, values_from = x, values_fill = "") %>%
  kable(caption = "Analysis plan: 46 treatment effects in 11 analytic samples") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("condensed"), font_size = 12)
```

## 3. Causal framework

Each student $i$ has two potential outcomes, $Y_i(1)$ under treatment and $Y_i(0)$
without it, and the estimand is the average treatment effect

$$\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}\left[Y(1) - Y(0)\right].$$

The ATE is identified from observational data under three assumptions.

* **Consistency.** The observed outcome equals the potential outcome under the treatment received.
* **Conditional exchangeability.** Given the measured covariates, treatment assignment is independent of the potential outcomes, so there is no unmeasured confounding.
* **Positivity.** Every student has a probability strictly between 0 and 1 of being in either group.

The assumed causal structure is shown below with GPA as the treatment. The same structure
is assumed for every other treatment, with the focal treatment taking the place of GPA and
all other measured variables treated as common causes of the treatment and the outcome.

```{r dag, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.2}
nodes <- data.frame(
  name = c("Demographics\n(age, gender, race,\nfirst generation)",
           "Academic context\n(field of study,\nhours worked)",
           "Support network\n(structure, closeness,\nhelp received)",
           "Perceived support\n(MSPSS, community)",
           "Psychosocial\n(perseverance, PTSD,\ntrauma, isolation)",
           "GPA ≤ 3.0", "Mental health\n(DASS-21)"),
  x = c(1, 2.5, 4, 5.5, 7, 2.5, 5.5),
  y = c(3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 1, 1),
  type = c(rep("Covariate", 5), "Treatment", "Outcome"))
edges <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = nodes$x[1:5], y = 2.72, xend = 2.62, yend = 1.3),
  data.frame(x = nodes$x[1:5], y = 2.72, xend = 5.38, yend = 1.3),
  data.frame(x = 3.15, y = 1, xend = 4.65, yend = 1))
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"),
               colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name, fill = type), key_glyph = "rect",
             size = 3, label.padding = unit(0.3, "lines"), colour = "grey15") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Covariate = "#EDF3F8", Treatment = "#FDD49E", Outcome = "#C7E9C0"),
                    name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.3, 7.7), ylim = c(0.5, 3.6)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

For each treatment, the propensity score model uses **all measured variables except**
the outcome, the self-reported effect of COVID-19 on mental health (`covid_mh`, a proxy for
the outcome), and the variable the treatment is built from. Because all variables were
measured in the same survey, some covariates may act as mediators for some treatments, and
the estimates should be read as effects under the stated assumptions.

## 4. Propensity scores and weights

Propensity scores $\hat p_i = \Pr(D_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i)$ are estimated with XGBoost,
separately within each analytic sample. The settings are deliberately conservative for
samples of this size.

```{r xgb-settings, echo = FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Setting, ~Value,
  "Objective", "binary:logistic (log loss)",
  "Learning rate (eta)", "0.05",
  "Maximum tree depth", "2",
  "Minimum child weight", "5",
  "Row and column subsampling", "0.8",
  "Number of rounds", "5-fold cross-validation, early stopping after 25 rounds, maximum 1000",
  "Final model", "Refit on the full analytic sample with the selected number of rounds",
  "Missing values (age only)", "Handled natively (learned default split direction)"
) %>% kable() %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = "condensed")
```

The core of the estimation in `R/causal_ipw.R`:

```{r core-code, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE, class.source = "fold-show"}
# Propensity scores, in the original row order
dall <- xgboost::xgb.DMatrix(data.matrix(X), label = D, missing = NA)
cv   <- xgboost::xgb.cv(params = xgb_params, data = dall, nrounds = 1000,
                        nfold = 5, early_stopping_rounds = 25, verbose = 0)
best <- which.min(cv$evaluation_log$test_logloss_mean)
fit  <- xgboost::xgb.train(params = xgb_params, data = dall, nrounds = best)
p    <- predict(fit, dall)

# Unstabilized, untruncated ATE weights
w <- ifelse(D == 1, 1 / p, 1 / (1 - p))

# Weighted least squares of the outcome on the treatment, HC2 standard errors
est <- estimatr::lm_robust(mh_scale ~ D, weights = w, se_type = "HC2", alpha = 0.10)
```

Because the treatment is the only regressor, the coefficient on `D` equals the
weighted difference in mean outcomes between the two groups, which is the IPW estimate of
the ATE. "Robust" refers only to the HC2 sandwich standard errors. Stabilizing the weights
would rescale them by a constant within each arm and leave the estimate unchanged.

## 5. Weighting diagnostics

### Balance, weights, and effective sample size (Supplementary Table S2)

Balance is measured by standardized mean differences (SMD), using the pooled standard
deviation of the two groups *before* weighting as the denominator, so that the before and
after columns are on the same scale. An absolute SMD below 0.1 indicates adequate balance.

```{r diag-table}
diag <- res %>%
  arrange(Group) %>%
  transmute(Group, Treatment,
            `Treated / control` = paste(n_treated, n_control, sep = " / "),
            `PS range` = sprintf("%.2f–%.2f", ps_min, ps_max),
            `Weight range` = sprintf("%.2f–%.2f", weight_min, weight_max),
            `ESS treated / control` = sprintf("%.0f / %.0f", ess_treated, ess_control),
            `Max |SMD| before` = round(max_abs_smd_before, 2),
            `Max |SMD| after`  = round(max_abs_smd_after, 2),
            `|SMD| > 0.1 before / after` = paste(n_smd_over_cutoff_before, n_smd_over_cutoff_after, sep = " / "))
kable(diag, caption = "Weighting diagnostics for all 46 analyses") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), font_size = 12) %>%
  collapse_rows(columns = 1, valign = "top") %>%
  scroll_box(height = "520px")
```

Across all analyses, the weights range from **`r sprintf("%.2f", min(res$weight_min))`
to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(res$weight_max))`**, and no propensity score is below
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(res$ps_min))` or above `r sprintf("%.3f", max(res$ps_max))`,
so there are no extreme weights. Weighting reduces imbalance, but some covariates retain
absolute SMDs above 0.1 in every analysis, which the paper acknowledges as a limitation.

### Covariate balance in the full sample

The plot shows, for each full-sample treatment, the 12 covariates with the largest
imbalance before weighting (all SMDs are in `output/balance.csv`, provided as S1 Data).

```{r love-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
full_bal <- bal %>%
  filter(group == "Full sample") %>%
  mutate(Treatment = unname(trt_labels[treatment])) %>%
  group_by(Treatment) %>%
  slice_max(abs(smd_before), n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_longer(c(smd_before, smd_after), names_to = "when", values_to = "smd") %>%
  mutate(when = factor(when, c("smd_before", "smd_after"), c("Before weighting", "After weighting")),
         covariate = reorder(paste(covariate, Treatment, sep = "___"), abs(smd)))
ggplot(full_bal, aes(abs(smd), covariate, colour = when)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(group = covariate), colour = "grey80") +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub("___.*$", "", x)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D95F02", "#1B9E77"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ Treatment, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Absolute standardized mean difference", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

### Overlap of propensity scores (Supplementary Fig S1)

Each panel shows the distribution of propensity scores among treated students (dark, upward)
and comparison students (light, downward). Overlap is good for most treatments and more
limited for PTSD symptom severity and educational help.

```{r overlap, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(sprintf("figures/overlap-%d.png", 1:4))
```

### A note on the smallest subgroups

In several small subgroups, cross-validation selected a model whose propensity scores
barely vary. In those analyses the weights are nearly constant within each arm, so the
weighted estimate is essentially the unadjusted difference in means. They are listed below
for transparency.

```{r flat-ps}
res %>%
  filter(ps_max - ps_min < 0.02) %>%
  transmute(Group, Treatment, n, `Treated / control` = paste(n_treated, n_control, sep = " / "),
            `PS range` = sprintf("%.3f–%.3f", ps_min, ps_max),
            `Weighted estimate` = round(estimate, 4),
            `Unadjusted difference` = round(raw_difference, 4)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Analyses with nearly constant propensity scores") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), font_size = 12)
```

## 6. Treatment effect estimates (Tables 3 to 7)

Estimates are in units of the Mental Health Scale (0 to 3). A positive estimate means the
treated group has *more* distress, and a negative estimate means *less* distress. The tables
report unadjusted p-values, Benjamini and Hochberg (BH) adjusted p-values, and 90% confidence
intervals. Rows significant after adjustment are in **bold**; rows significant only before
adjustment are in *italics*.

```{r result-tables, results = "asis"}
make_table <- function(groups, caption) {
  d <- res %>% filter(Group %in% groups) %>% arrange(Group)
  out <- d %>% transmute(Group, Treatment,
                         Estimate = sprintf("%.4f", estimate),
                         `P-value` = fmt_p(p_value),
                         `BH p-value` = fmt_p(p_value_BH),
                         `90% CI` = sprintf("(%.4f, %.4f)", ci_lower, ci_upper))
  k <- kable(out %>% select(-Group), caption = caption, align = "lrrrr") %>%
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("condensed", "hover"))
  bold <- which(d$p_value_BH < alpha); ital <- which(d$p_value < alpha & d$p_value_BH >= alpha)
  if (length(bold)) k <- row_spec(k, bold, bold = TRUE)
  if (length(ital)) k <- row_spec(k, ital, italic = TRUE)
  for (g in unique(as.character(d$Group))) {
    idx <- which(as.character(d$Group) == g)
    if (length(groups) > 1) k <- pack_rows(k, g, min(idx), max(idx))
  }
  print(k)
}
make_table("Full sample", "Table 3. Full sample")
make_table(c("High PTSD symptom severity", "Low PTSD symptom severity"), "Table 4. Stratified by PTSD symptom severity")
make_table(c("Cisgender women", "Cisgender men"), "Table 5. Stratified by gender identity")
make_table(c("White students", "Asian/Asian-American students", "Students of other racial identities"),
           "Table 6. Stratified by race")
make_table(c("Ages 18–20", "Ages 21–24", "Ages 25+"), "Table 7. Stratified by age")
```

### All 46 estimates at a glance

```{r forest, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 11}
res %>%
  mutate(sig = case_when(p_value_BH < alpha ~ "Significant after BH adjustment",
                         p_value < alpha    ~ "Significant before adjustment only",
                         TRUE               ~ "Not significant"),
         sig = factor(sig, c("Significant after BH adjustment",
                             "Significant before adjustment only", "Not significant"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(estimate, reorder(Treatment, estimate), colour = sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = ci_lower, xmax = ci_upper), height = 0.25) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Group, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_wrap_gen(28)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#08519C", "#6BAED6", "grey65"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Estimated effect on the Mental Health Scale (90% CI)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

Two patterns stand out. PTSD symptom severity is associated with substantially greater
distress in the full sample and in every gender, racial, and age subgroup in which it was
examined, and having three or more educational helpers is associated with less distress in
the full sample and most subgroups. The subgroup analyses are exploratory and the subgroups
were not formally compared.

### Checks on the reported intervals

Every 90% confidence interval is symmetric about its estimate, with half-width equal to
the 95th percentile of the $t$ distribution with $n - 2$ degrees of freedom times the HC2
standard error, as computed by `estimatr::lm_robust`.

```{r ci-check}
res %>%
  summarise(`Max |midpoint - estimate|` = max(abs((ci_lower + ci_upper) / 2 - estimate)),
            `Max |half-width - t x SE|` = max(abs((ci_upper - ci_lower) / 2 -
                                                qt(1 - alpha / 2, n - 2) * std_error))) %>%
  kable(digits = 8) %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

## 7. The Benjamini and Hochberg adjustment

The BH procedure controls the false discovery rate across all $m = 46$ estimates. With the
unadjusted p-values sorted as $p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}$, the adjusted value at rank $i$ is

$$\tilde p_{(i)} = \min_{j \ge i} \left\{ \frac{m}{j}\, p_{(j)} \right\},$$

capped at 1. The step below recomputes the adjustment from the unadjusted p-values and
confirms that it matches the values in the tables.

```{r bh-check, echo = TRUE, class.source = "fold-show"}
bh <- p.adjust(res$p_value, method = "BH")
all.equal(bh, res$p_value_BH)
```

The table shows ranks 13 to 22, where the running minimum matters. At ranks 13, 20 and 21
the raw value $m\,p_{(i)}/i$ is larger than a value at a higher rank, so the adjusted
p-value is pulled down to that later value. This is why several rows in Tables 4 to 6
share an adjusted p-value of 0.1034.

```{r bh-example}
m <- nrow(res)
res %>%
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  mutate(Rank = row_number(), `m p / rank` = p_value * m / Rank) %>%
  slice(13:22) %>%
  transmute(Rank, Group, Treatment, `P-value` = round(p_value, 4),
            `m p / rank` = round(`m p / rank`, 4), `BH p-value` = round(p_value_BH, 4)) %>%
  kable() %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), font_size = 12)
```

For example, isolation in the full sample has an unadjusted p-value of 0.0360 at rank 18,
so its adjusted p-value is $0.0360 \times 46 / 18 = 0.0920$, which remains below
$\alpha = 0.10$.
